notes.meaning: God himself speaks these laws to Moses. Many different rules follow, but they all share one purpose: that God's people should be holy. They are to shape their worship by who God is, not by their own ideas.

Moses must tell these laws to the whole people, not just to the priests. Everyone needed to know their duty. To be holy means to be set apart from sin and the world and given fully to God. The reason is simple: God is holy, and his children should be like their Father. Peter repeats this call to Christians in 1 Peter 1:15-16.

To "respect" parents means honor, reverence, and obedience, as in the fifth of the Ten Commandments. The mother is named first to show she is owed the same honor as the father. Grown children still owe this respect. Keeping the Sabbath (God's weekly day of rest and worship) is joined to it, because parents should lead their homes in honoring God. If parents ever pull children away from God's day, God's command comes first.

The word for idols means "nothings." False gods have no power to help or harm. God's people must not turn their eyes or hearts to them. "Molten gods" are statues made from melted metal, which recalls the golden calf. This verse sums up the first two of the Ten Commandments.

A peace offering was a sacrifice shared as a meal. Part went to the priests, and the worshiper and his friends ate the rest. It was given freely, of the person's own choice. Still, it had to be offered God's way to be accepted.

The meat had to be eaten the same day or the next day. Anything left by the third day had to be burned. This rule may have kept people from treating leftover holy meat as if it had magic power. God wanted his own work done in his own time.

Meat eaten on the third day was spoiled in God's eyes, and he would not accept the offering. The person who ate it treated a holy thing as common. He would carry his own guilt and be cut off from God's people. Even a sacrifice offered rightly was no good if the people did not finish their part rightly.

At harvest, farmers had to leave the edges of the field uncut. They could not go back for grain or grapes they had missed or dropped. These were left for the poor and for foreigners. This was a very early law to care for the poor, and Ruth gathered grain this way. It teaches us not to be greedy, to be glad when the poor share in our blessings, and to remember that all we have comes from God.

God forbids stealing, whether by open theft or by cheating. This includes denying you have something a person trusted you to keep. God also forbids lying to one another, in business or in daily talk. Paul repeats this for Christians: "Do not lie to one another."

It is bad to tell a lie, but much worse to swear to it in God's name. One sin easily leads to another, and a liar may soon become a false swearer. God's name must also not be used lightly or carelessly.

Do not cheat your neighbor or take what is his by force. A day worker must be paid the same day. Poor workers live from hand to mouth, and their families need that money right away. Holding back their pay is a serious sin that cries out to God (James 5:4).

Do not curse a deaf person, who cannot hear you or defend himself. Do not trip up a blind person. This covers anyone too weak to protect themselves, and it implies we should help them. People may not fear the deaf or the blind, but they must fear God, who sees and hears and defends the helpless. Jewish teachers also read it as a warning not to give bad advice to simple people.

Judges and anyone settling a dispute must be fair. They must not favor the poor out of pity or the rich out of fear or respect. The case should be decided on its facts, not on who the people are. James 2:1-4 teaches the same.

The word for a slanderer pictures a peddler who goes from house to house trading in gossip. God forbids spreading stories that hurt people's good name. He also forbids putting a neighbor's life in danger, for example as a false witness in court. Jewish teachers added that we should not stand by when a neighbor is in danger.

God cares about the heart, not just actions. Hidden hatred is like murder begun (1 John 3:15). Instead of nursing a grudge, speak to the person directly. Gently show them their fault, ideally in private, as Jesus teaches in Matthew 18:15. Loving correction helps them turn from sin, and it keeps you from sharing in their guilt.

Do not pay back wrongs or keep bringing them up. Forgive, as God forgives us. Instead, love your neighbor as yourself. Jesus called this the second great commandment, and Paul says it sums up our duty to others. "Neighbor" means every person, as Jesus showed in the story of the Good Samaritan. The point is not to love ourselves first, but to care for others as sincerely as we care for ourselves.

Israel was not to crossbreed animals, plant two kinds of seed together, or wear cloth woven of wool and linen. God made each kind separate at creation, and his people were to respect that order. These rules also taught Israel not to mix with the nations or blend pagan ways into God's worship. Matthew Henry counts this among the laws that were only for Israel.

Here a man sleeps with a slave woman who is promised in marriage to another man. Such adultery was punished, often by whipping. It was not punished by death, because she was not yet free. Marriage, even when only promised, was to be honored.

The man also had to bring a ram as a guilt offering, a sacrifice for wrongdoing. The priest made atonement for him, meaning the sin was covered and he was put right with God. Then he was forgiven. Needing a sacrifice shows this was no small sin, even though the earthly penalty was lighter.

For three years, the fruit of a newly planted tree was "forbidden," like something unclean. People were not to eat it. Gardeners know young trees grow stronger when early fruit is picked off. The rule also taught God's people to control their appetites and wait patiently.

In the fourth year, all the fruit belonged to God as a praise offering. It was like the firstfruits, given to thank him for making the trees grow. It went to the priests or was eaten joyfully before the Lord.
From the fifth year on, the people could eat the fruit. God promised that their patience would be repaid with bigger harvests. Only God's blessing makes trees fruitful.

Do not eat meat with the blood still in it. Pagans did this in rites to share a meal with their gods. Do not try to read the future by signs, such as snakes or clouds, or treat some days as lucky and others unlucky. Such practices show a lack of trust in God's care. Christians should also stay away from fortune-telling and charms.

Israel's neighbors cut their hair and beards in special ways. They did this to honor their gods or to show wild grief. God forbade these customs to keep his people separate from idol worship, even in how they looked.

Pagans gashed their bodies when someone died, hoping to please the gods of death. They also marked their skin to honor their idols. God's people were not to copy these practices. Christians can grieve with hope, because Christ has changed what death means for those who trust him.

Some pagans gave their daughters to prostitution, even as part of worship. God forbids this evil. Such sin spreads until the whole land is full of wickedness. More broadly, parents should raise their children in purity, and all sex outside marriage is wrong in God's sight.

God's people must keep his day of rest and show deep respect for his house of worship. The Sabbath and worship at the sanctuary went together. Doing both guarded them against pagan ways. For Christians, it means treating church gatherings with reverence, since Christ promises to be present there.

Mediums claimed to talk with the dead or with spirits. Spiritists claimed to tell the future. God's people must not seek them out for advice, hope, or fear. Doing so dishonors God and makes a person unclean. This sin helped bring about King Saul's downfall.

Stand up when an older person comes by, and honor the aged. Old age is a gift from God and deserves respect for his sake. Their wisdom and advice should be valued. Even common sense teaches this, and faith teaches good manners.

Foreigners living in Israel must not be mistreated, cheated, or insulted. They are to be treated like native-born people and loved as oneself. Israel once lived as foreigners in Egypt, so they knew how it felt. God takes special care of those who have no one to defend them. This shows that "neighbor" includes everyone.

Buyers and sellers must use honest rulers, scales, and weights. An ephah measured dry goods like grain, and a hin measured liquids. These two stand for all measures. Cheating with false weights is like robbery dressed up as fairness, and God hates it. God reminds them he is the one who freed them from Egypt, so they should gladly obey him.

The chapter ends with a call to keep all of God's laws, not just some of them. We must study them carefully and then truly obey them. "I am the LORD" is repeated many times in this chapter. It reminds us that God is our Maker, Rescuer, and King, so he has every right to our obedience. His blessings are not an excuse to sin but a reason to obey.
